```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.pos = "htbp")
template_dir <- "../../_shared/template"
source(file.path(template_dir, "viscount_rmd_helpers.R"))
library(jsonlite)

read_json5_clean <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  lines <- gsub("//.*$", "", lines)
  txt <- paste(lines, collapse = "\n")
  txt <- gsub("/\\*.*?\\*/", "", txt, perl = TRUE)
  txt <- gsub(",\\s*([}\\]])", "\\1", txt, perl = TRUE)
  fromJSON(txt, simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

mod_data <- read_json5_clean("chile_rio_plata_banda_oriental.json5")
sum_data <- fromJSON("chile_rio_plata_banda_oriental_summary.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
sett_data <- fromJSON("chile_rio_plata_banda_oriental_settlements.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
enum_data <- sum_data
```

# Abstract

This study reconstructs the population trajectory, administrative geography and urban hierarchy of the Captaincy General of Chile, the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata south of the Pilcomayo and Uruguay headwaters, and the Banda Oriental from the first Spanish incursions of 1536 to the consolidation of the post-colonial republics in 1830. Across eight territorial units spanning 3.511.387 km² and 52.269 raster cells, aggregate population fell steeply from 1,66M (1.655.000) in 1536 to 993k in 1600 and 819k in 1650 under epidemic mortality, forced *encomienda* labour and frontier warfare [@valenzuelamarquez2014indios; @boccara1999poder; @bixio2019reflexiones]. Demographic contraction bottomed near 791k around 1700, after which agrarian expansion in Chile's Central Valley, mule and textile commerce linking Tucumán to Potosí, and Bourbon maritime liberalisation at Buenos Aires and Montevideo lifted the regional total to 875.159 in 1778, 1,38M in 1813 and 1,77M (1.767.000) by 1830 [@kamen1974mecanismes; @socolow1978merchants; @fuce2017real; @gelman1905campesinos]. Reconciling the 1777 to 1778 Chilean *Censo de Jáuregui* (240.748 in the Bishopric of Santiago excluding Cuyo) and the 1778 *Censo de Vértiz* (186.526 enumerated across core Río de la Plata jurisdictions) with the 1791 to 1793 O'Higgins ecclesiastical rolls, the 1813 Egaña census and missionary records from the Paraná-Uruguay Guaraní reductions anchors the colonial demographic curve [@jackson2015managing; @escolar2021liderazgo; @pollero2015que]. Simultaneously, the Gran Chaco (185k to 76k) and Patagonia with the southern Pampas (110k to 46k) remained largely autonomous indigenous frontiers whose inhabitants experienced protracted attrition rather than direct colonial enumeration [@dillehay2016reflections; @gandara2016representaciones]. Across the 177 catalogued settlements, led by Buenos Aires (55,4k in 1822), Santiago (54k in 1830), Valparaíso (18k) and Montevideo (15,2k), urbanisation remained modest overall yet redistributed the centre of demographic gravity from the Andean interior toward the Atlantic estuary and the central Chilean ports [@johnson2011workshop; @goldberg1976poblacion].

# Background

## Spanish Conquest and Colonial Partition of the Southern Cone (1536 to 1776)

European occupation of the Southern Cone proceeded along two distinct corridors that converged only slowly across the cordillera and the interior plains. From Peru, Diego de Almagro marched south across the Atacama in 1536 before Pedro de Valdivia founded Santiago del Nuevo Extremo in February 1541, establishing the nucleus of the Captaincy General of Chile alongside La Serena (1544), Concepción (1550) and Valdivia (1552) [@valenzuelamarquez2014indios; @boccara1999poder]. Across the Andes, expeditions descending from Charcas and Peru founded Santiago del Estero (1553), San Miguel de Tucumán (1565), Córdoba (1573), Salta (1582) and San Salvador de Jujuy (1593), while trans-Andean columns from Chile established Mendoza (1561), San Juan (1562) and San Luis (1594) in the Corregimiento de Cuyo [@bixio2019reflexiones; @marschoff2018movilidad; @escolar2021liderazgo]. On the Atlantic littoral, Pedro de Mendoza's short-lived settlement of 1536 succumbed to starvation and Querandí hostility, leaving Spanish presence anchored upriver at Asunción until Juan de Garay founded Santa Fe (1573) and refounded Buenos Aires in 1580 [@pelozattoreilly2016mano; @molina2018militarizacion].

Throughout the Habsburg centuries, the political geography of the region remained fragmented and peripheral to Lima. Chile and Tucumán depended juridically on the Viceroyalty of Peru, yet their demographic and economic circuits operated along divergent axes [@kamen1974mecanismes; @bixio2019reflexiones]. Central Chile evolved around wheat, tallow and wine estates (*estancias* and *haciendas*) exporting surplus provisions to the Peruvian coast through Valparaíso, while southern Chile collapsed into a militarised frontier after the great Mapuche uprising of 1598 destroyed all seven Spanish towns south of the Biobío River except Castro on Chiloé Island [@boccara1999poder; @dillehay2016reflections]. East of the Andes, the Gobernación del Tucumán functioned as an agrarian and pastoral supplier to the silver mines of Potosí, breeding tens of thousands of mules in Córdoba and Salta and weaving coarse cottons and woollens for Upper Peruvian markets [@bixio2019reflexiones; @marschoff2018movilidad]. By contrast, Buenos Aires persisted as a modest port whose legal commerce was choked by Lima's Seville-Portobelo monopoly, forcing local merchants and officials into endemic contraband trade with Portuguese Colonia del Sacramento and Brazil [@socolow1978merchants; @silva1997bases].

## The Bourbon Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata and Late-Colonial Reforms (1776 to 1830)

The strategic vulnerability of the South Atlantic estuary to Portuguese and British encroachment compelled the Bourbon Crown to redraw the colonial map in 1776. Creating the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata detached Upper Peru, Paraguay, Tucumán, Buenos Aires and Cuyo from Lima, placing Potosí's silver shipments directly through the port of Buenos Aires [@socolow1978merchants; @molina2018militarizacion]. Two years later, the Regulation of Free Trade (*Comercio Libre*) of 1778 legalised direct commerce between Iberian ports and both Buenos Aires and Montevideo, while Cuyo was permanently transferred from Chile to the new viceregal orbit [@escolar2021liderazgo; @martinschlez2016medicion]. In the Banda Oriental, where Spanish authorities had founded the fortified *Real* of San Felipe y Santiago de Montevideo between 1724 and 1726 to counter the Portuguese enclave at Colonia del Sacramento, Bourbon naval investment and cattle ranching transformed a garrison outpost into the viceroyalty's premier deep-water port [@fuce2017real; @gelman1905campesinos].

Administrative restructuring coincided with an unprecedented wave of demographic counting and frontier surveillance. In Chile, Governor Agustín de Jáuregui ordered a comprehensive census of the Bishopric of Santiago in 1777 to 1778, followed by Ambrosio O'Higgins's ecclesiastical *matrículas* of 1791 to 1793 and Juan Egaña's republican-era survey of 1813 [@kamen1974mecanismes; @gandara2016representaciones]. In the Río de la Plata, Viceroy Juan José de Vértiz executed the 1778 household enumeration across Buenos Aires, Córdoba, Tucumán, Salta, Jujuy, Catamarca and Cuyo, supplemented by municipal *padrones* in Montevideo during the 1770s and early nineteenth century [@pollero2015que; @johnson2011workshop]. After 1810, independence wars ruptured viceregal unity: Buenos Aires's May Revolution severed the Platine basin from Potosí's silver, José de San Martín's Army of the Andes drew manpower from Cuyo and Chile, and the Banda Oriental endured Luso-Brazilian occupation before emerging as Uruguay in 1828 to 1830 [@molina2018militarizacion; @silva1997bases; @gelman1905campesinos].

# Methodology

## Sub-Regional Partition and Spatial Masking

To preserve administrative fidelity across shifting colonial and early republican borders between 1536 and 1830, the study domain is partitioned into eight contiguous territorial units covering 3.511.387 km² across 52.269 grid cells (equivalent to 3.574.522 km² in the vector subregion geometry). Each unit reflects a distinct ecological, juridical and demographic regime rather than modern twentieth-century departmental lines. The Captaincy General of Chile comprises the Obispado de Santiago (209.632 km², stretching from Copiapó and the Atacama margin to the Maule River) and the Obispado de Concepción, Araucanía and Chiloé (379.064 km², encompassing the northern Biobío frontier towns, the autonomous Mapuche heartland between the Biobío and Toltén rivers, the Valdivia enclave and the Chiloé archipelago). Across the cordillera, the Corregimiento de Cuyo (202.256 km², uniting the oasis towns of Mendoza, San Juan and San Luis) is treated separately because its demographic history straddled Chilean jurisdiction until 1776 and the Río de la Plata thereafter [@escolar2021liderazgo].

East of Cuyo and north of the Salado River, four units capture the Platine and interior provinces. The Gobernación del Tucumán (504.641 km²) brings together the colonial jurisdictions of Córdoba, Santiago del Estero, San Miguel de Tucumán, Catamarca, La Rioja, Salta and Jujuy along the Potosí overland highway [@bixio2019reflexiones; @marschoff2018movilidad]. The Intendencia de Buenos Aires (244.799 km²) covers the Buenos Aires city and *campaña*, Santa Fe, Entre Ríos and Corrientes along the Paraná axis [@pelozattoreilly2016mano; @contente2017numeros]. The Banda Oriental del Uruguay and Misiones (263.007 km²) pairs the eastern estuary littoral around Montevideo and Colonia with the Upper Paraná and Uruguay Jesuit-Guaraní mission districts [@fuce2017real; @kuhne2025churches; @jackson2015managing]. Finally, two autonomous indigenous macro-territories are masked separately so unenumerated populations are never conflated with colonial tax rolls: the Gran Chaco Indigenous Frontier (425.650 km²) and the Patagonia and Southern Pampas Indigenous Frontier (1.282.338 km²) [@dillehay2016reflections; @gandara2016representaciones].

## Benchmark Construction and Reconciling Colonial Enumerations

Population series are anchored at seven chronological benchmarks: 1536, 1600, 1650, 1700, 1778, 1813 and 1830. The primary colonial pivot lies at 1778, where the Jáuregui enumeration in Chile and the Vértiz census in the Río de la Plata overlap closely in time. For the Obispado de Santiago, the published 1777 to 1778 Jáuregui summary records 259.646 inhabitants across its ten constituent *corregimientos*, including 18.898 in Cuyo (Mendoza). Subtracting Cuyo leaves 240.748 inhabitants in Central and Northern Chile proper, matching our exact 1778 benchmark for the Obispado de Santiago. For Cuyo itself, the 1778 Vértiz returns specify 8.765 in Mendoza, 7.690 in San Juan and 6.956 in San Luis, summing to 23.411 inhabitants, which provides the exact 1778 benchmark for the Corregimiento de Cuyo.

Where eighteenth-century enumerations omitted rural peripheries, fugitive slaves, ecclesiastical immunities or frontier populations, historical multipliers are applied in line with regional demographic scholarship. In the Obispado de Concepción, where Spanish counts covered only the northern Maule-to-Biobío strip, Valdivia and Chiloé (recorded at 105.114 in the 1791 to 1793 O'Higgins *matrículas*), adding an estimated 110k autonomous Mapuche, Pewenche and Williche inhabitants yields 215k in 1778 [@boccara1999poder; @dillehay2016reflections; @gandara2016representaciones]. In the Intendencia de Buenos Aires and the Gobernación del Tucumán, raw Vértiz totals omit several jurisdictions such as Santiago del Estero, Santa Fe, Corrientes and La Rioja, and under-enumerate dispersed rural *peones* and *campaña* squatters; adding archival parish and cabildo estimates raises Buenos Aires to 58k and Tucumán to 138k in 1778 [@gelman1905campesinos; @pelozattoreilly2016mano; @contente2017numeros]. In the Banda Oriental and Misiones, post-1767 mission contraction from over 100k Guaraní neophytes in the 1730s to roughly 20k by the late 1770s is combined with 18k to 22k Spanish, mestizo and enslaved residents in Montevideo, Colonia and the pastoral countryside to give 42k in 1778 [@jackson2015managing; @perezgerardo2022practicas; @pollero2015que].

Pre-1778 benchmarks (1536, 1600, 1650 and 1700) draw on early *visitas*, *encomienda* tribute rolls, Jesuit *annuae* and ethnohistoric carrying-capacity reconstructions across each ecological zone [@valenzuelamarquez2014indios; @bixio2019reflexiones; @jackson2015managing]. Post-1778 benchmarks (1813 and 1830) bridge the 1813 Egaña Chilean survey (823.685 projected across Chile's central and southern provinces, adjusted downward in Concepción for autonomous Mapuche numbers separately tracked in our series), provincial Buenos Aires and Córdoba counts of 1812 to 1822, and early republican parish reconstructions [@kamen1974mecanismes; @goldberg1976poblacion; @pollero2015que]. Uncertainty bands of $\pm 16\%$ around every sub-regional estimate express plausible upper and lower bounds ($0,84\,P$ to $1,16\,P$) across pre-statistical and partial-census horizons.

# Testing and Validation

## Reconciliation of the 1777 to 1778 Bourbon Censuses

The Bourbon enumerations of 1777 to 1778 offer the earliest cross-continental snapshot of socio-racial composition and sub-administrative distribution across the Southern Cone. Table \ref{tab:census-jauregui} reproduces the full nine-*corregimiento* breakdown of the 1777 to 1778 Jáuregui census for the Obispado de Santiago alongside the official diocesan aggregate. Two structural features stand out immediately. First, the sum of the nine tabulated *corregimientos* (193.934) falls 65.712 short of the official diocesan total (259.646), reflecting omitted rural *doctrinas* and the Copiapó-Huasco northern mining belt in the surviving partial table, which raises the *españoles* category from 130.654 to 190.889 in the consolidated diocesan return. Second, *españoles* (combining peninsulars, *criollos* and assimilated *mestizos* passing into white fiscal status) comprised 73,5% of the official diocesan total, whereas *indios* (8,7%) and *negros* with *mulatos* (9,8%) concentrated heavily in Santiago itself and in Cuyo [@valenzuelamarquez2014indios; @kamen1974mecanismes].

```{r tab-jauregui, results='asis'}
j_raw <- enum_data$colonial_enumerations$chile_1777_1778_and_1813$censo_1777_1778_obispado_santiago
corr_names <- names(j_raw$corregimientos)
j_rows <- lapply(corr_names, function(cn) {
  it <- j_raw$corregimientos[[cn]]
  data.frame(
    Jurisdiction = cn,
    Espanoles = viscount_fmt_number(it$espanoles, 0L),
    Mestizos = viscount_fmt_number(it$mestizos, 0L),
    Indios = viscount_fmt_number(it$indios, 0L),
    Negros = viscount_fmt_number(it$negros, 0L),
    Total = viscount_fmt_number(it$total, 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
j_df <- do.call(rbind, j_rows)
j_df <- rbind(
  j_df,
  data.frame(
    Jurisdiction = "Sum of 9 Corregimientos",
    Espanoles = viscount_fmt_number(j_raw$sum_corregimientos$espanoles, 0L),
    Mestizos = viscount_fmt_number(j_raw$sum_corregimientos$mestizos, 0L),
    Indios = viscount_fmt_number(j_raw$sum_corregimientos$indios, 0L),
    Negros = viscount_fmt_number(j_raw$sum_corregimientos$negros, 0L),
    Total = viscount_fmt_number(j_raw$sum_corregimientos$total, 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ),
  data.frame(
    Jurisdiction = "Official Obispado Total",
    Espanoles = viscount_fmt_number(j_raw$official_obispado_total$espanoles, 0L),
    Mestizos = viscount_fmt_number(j_raw$official_obispado_total$mestizos, 0L),
    Indios = viscount_fmt_number(j_raw$official_obispado_total$indios, 0L),
    Negros = viscount_fmt_number(j_raw$official_obispado_total$negros, 0L),
    Total = viscount_fmt_number(j_raw$official_obispado_total$total, 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
)
rownames(j_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  j_df,
  "Sub-administrative returns from the 1777 to 1778 Censo de Jáuregui across the Obispado de Santiago.",
  c("Corregimiento", "Españoles", "Mestizos", "Indios", "Negros", "Total"),
  list(label = "tab:census-jauregui", font_size = "footnotesize")
)
```

East of the Andes, Table \ref{tab:census-vertiz} compiles the fourteen jurisdictional returns and historiographical ranges from the 1778 *Censo de Vértiz* across the newly erected Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata. The explicitly enumerated jurisdictions sum to 186.526 inhabitants, dominated by Córdoba (44.506, of which roughly 84% lived in rural *curatos*), Buenos Aires city and *campaña* (37.679, with 24.205 to 24.754 inside the urban perimeter), Tucumán (20.104) and Catamarca (15.315) [@bixio2019reflexiones; @johnson2011workshop]. Crucially, the Vértiz figures reveal the interior's continued demographic weight in 1778: the combined Tucumán jurisdictions far outnumbered Buenos Aires, while Catamarca's casta majority (7.908 *castas* against 4.567 *blancos* and 2.817 *indios*) exemplifies the deep Afro-indigenous admixture of the northwestern valleys [@marschoff2018movilidad].

Table \ref{tab:chile-late-censuses} juxtaposes the three principal late-colonial and early-independence enumerations for the Captaincy General of Chile: the 1777 to 1778 Jáuregui census, the 1791 to 1793 O'Higgins ecclesiastical *matrículas*, and the 1813 Egaña survey [@kamen1974mecanismes; @gandara2016representaciones]. While the O'Higgins rolls recorded 203.732 souls in the Bishopric of Santiago and 105.114 in the Bishopric of Concepción (a narrower parish perimeter excluding unsubdued Mapuche territories), the 1813 Egaña compilation yielded 823.685 across Chile as a whole (400.525 men and 423.160 women, including Coquimbo at roughly 29k and retrospective projections for Santiago and Concepción where war interrupted field enumeration) [@kamen1974mecanismes; @boccara1999poder].

## Arithmetic Consistency and Gazetteer Coverage

Cross-checking the sub-regional aggregates in Table \ref{tab:subregions-crp} confirms exact arithmetic closure across all seven benchmark years: summing the eight individual territories reproduces the headline totals of 1,66M (1536), 993k (1600), 819k (1650), 791k (1700), 875.159 (1778), 1,38M (1813) and 1,77M (1830). Every one of the eight masked territories contains at least one geocoded settlement from the 177-entry gazetteer, achieving zero unaccounted sub-regions and zero reliance on crowdsourced fallback records [@marschoff2018movilidad; @contente2017numeros]. In Wave 4 gap checks, newly added frontier settlements contributed a marginal gain of 1,14%, confirming archival saturation across the three constituent modern republics (87 sites in Argentina, 59 in Chile and 31 in Uruguay).

# Results

## Long-Run Demographic Trajectory (1536 to 1830)

The demographic history of Chile, the Río de la Plata and the Banda Oriental across the colonial centuries forms an asymmetric U-shaped curve: two centuries of indigenous contraction and sluggish Hispanic settlement followed by a sharp late-colonial and early republican surge (Figure \ref{fig:traj-crp}; Table \ref{tab:subregions-crp}). At contact in 1536, approximately 1,66M people inhabited the region, over half of them concentrated in southern Chile south of the Maule and in the sedentary agricultural valleys of Tucumán [@valenzuelamarquez2014indios; @bixio2019reflexiones; @dillehay2016reflections]. By 1600, Old World epidemics of smallpox, measles and typhus, compounded by *encomienda* mining drafts and war along the Biobío and Calchaquí valleys, had cut the total by 40,0% to 993k [@valenzuelamarquez2014indios; @boccara1999poder]. The decline continued through the seventeenth century, reaching 819k in 1650 and bottoming out at 791k in 1700, less than half the 1536 baseline [@kamen1974mecanismes; @marschoff2018movilidad].

```{r fig-traj, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/chile_rio_plata_banda_oriental_population_trajectory.png",
  "Sub-regional demographic trajectory from 1536 to 1830 and comparative population density in 1830 across eight Southern Cone territories.",
  "fig:traj-crp"
)
```

Recovery began unevenly during the early eighteenth century and accelerated decisively after 1760. Between 1700 and 1778, total population edged upward by 10,6% from 791k to 875.159 as rapid Hispanic-mestizo natural growth in Central Chile (+55,3%) and Buenos Aires (+28,9%) more than offset continued attrition in the Chaco, Patagonia and the post-expulsion Guaraní missions [@kamen1974mecanismes; @jackson2015managing; @pelozattoreilly2016mano]. Between 1778 and 1813, the region added over 500k inhabitants (+57,2% to 1,38M), driven by commercial integration with the Atlantic, agrarian colonisation across the Central Valley and the Buenos Aires *campaña*, and forced African slave imports into the Platine ports [@socolow1978merchants; @goldberg1976poblacion; @gelman1905campesinos]. Despite severe military dislocation during the independence wars between 1810 and 1824, expansion persisted to 1,77M by 1830, surpassing the pre-contact population for the first time after nearly three centuries [@molina2018militarizacion; @contente2017numeros].

```{r tab-subregions, results='asis'}
yrs <- c("1536", "1600", "1650", "1700", "1778", "1813", "1830")
reg_short_map <- c(
  crp_obispado_santiago = "Obispado de Santiago",
  crp_obispado_concepcion_chiloe = "Obispado de Concepción and Chiloé",
  crp_corregimiento_cuyo = "Corregimiento de Cuyo",
  crp_intendencia_buenos_aires = "Intendencia de Buenos Aires",
  crp_banda_oriental_misiones = "Banda Oriental and Misiones",
  crp_gobernacion_tucuman = "Gobernación del Tucumán",
  crp_gran_chaco_frontier = "Gran Chaco Frontier",
  crp_patagonia_pampas_frontier = "Patagonia and Pampas Frontier"
)

sub_rows <- lapply(names(mod_data$regions), function(rk) {
  rv <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  nm <- unname(reg_short_map[rk])
  row_df <- data.frame(
    Territory = nm,
    Area = viscount_fmt_number(rv$area_km2, 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  for (y in yrs) {
    val <- as.numeric(rv$population[[y]])
    row_df[[y]] <- if (y == "1778" && rk %in% c("crp_obispado_santiago", "crp_corregimiento_cuyo")) {
      viscount_fmt_number(val, 0L)
    } else {
      viscount_fmt_pop(val)
    }
  }
  row_df
})
sub_df <- do.call(rbind, sub_rows)

tot_row <- data.frame(
  Territory = "Regional Total",
  Area = viscount_fmt_number(mod_data$total_area_km2, 0L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
for (y in yrs) {
  val <- as.numeric(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[[y]])
  tot_row[[y]] <- if (y == "1778") viscount_fmt_number(val, 0L) else viscount_fmt_pop(val)
}
sub_df <- rbind(sub_df, tot_row)
rownames(sub_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  sub_df,
  "Population benchmarks from 1536 to 1830 across the eight territorial divisions of Chile, the Río de la Plata and the Banda Oriental.",
  c("Territory", "Area (km²)", "1536", "1600", "1650", "1700", "1778", "1813", "1830"),
  list(label = "tab:subregions-crp", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Regional Trajectories across the Andes and Estuary

### Central and Northern Chile: The Obispado de Santiago

The Obispado de Santiago (209.632 km²) experienced the earliest and most sustained colonial recovery in the Southern Cone [@kamen1974mecanismes; @valenzuelamarquez2014indios]. Following an initial collapse from 260k in 1536 to 128k in 1650 as central *encomienda* communities shrank under gold-panning drafts, epidemic outbreaks and forced transfers from Cuyo and Chiloé, demographic growth resumed after 1650 [@valenzuelamarquez2014indios]. The great 1687 Peruvian earthquake triggered a sustained wheat export boom from the Aconcagua, Maipo and Maule valleys to Lima, converting Central Valley pastures into irrigated *haciendas* worked by resident *inquilino* tenant families [@kamen1974mecanismes]. Population climbed from 155k in 1700 to 240.748 in 1778, surged to 465k in 1813 and reached 585k by 1830, attaining 2,79 inhabitants per km² (2,78 on the vector geometry, the highest density in the entire study area) [@kamen1974mecanismes; @gandara2016representaciones].

### Southern Chile, Araucanía and Chiloé

South of the Maule, the Obispado de Concepción, Araucanía and Chiloé (379.064 km²) followed an altogether different trajectory governed by armed frontier coexistence [@boccara1999poder; @dillehay2016reflections]. Dense late pre-Columbian horticultural settlements supported roughly 590k inhabitants in 1536, but devastating war with Valdivia and García Hurtado de Mendoza, followed by the 1598 Mapuche counter-offensive and seventeenth-century slave raids (*malocas*), reduced total population to 310k in 1600 and 205k in 1700 [@boccara1999poder; @boccara1999politicas]. After the Crown formalised the Biobío border through periodic diplomatic *parlamentos* beginning at Quillín in 1641, cross-frontier livestock and poncho commerce stabilised Mapuche *lof* and *rewe* societies, keeping regional numbers near 215k in 1778 before Bourbon colonisation around Chillán, Los Ángeles and Valdivia alongside Chiloé growth lifted the total to 295k in 1813 and 375k in 1830 [@boccara1999poder; @dillehay2016reflections; @gandara2016representaciones].

### The Corregimiento de Cuyo

Cuyo (202.256 km²) formed a desert-oasis bridge linking Santiago to Córdoba and Buenos Aires [@escolar2021liderazgo]. Its original Huarpe population, estimated at 65k in 1536, suffered severe attrition not only from epidemics but from annual forced *mita* labour gangs marched over the Uspallata pass to work Santiago estates and mines, reducing Cuyo to 38k in 1600, 26k in 1650 and 22k in 1700 [@valenzuelamarquez2014indios; @escolar2021liderazgo]. Viticulture, dried-fruit production and cart freightage revived the irrigated valleys of Mendoza and San Juan during the eighteenth century, yielding 23.411 inhabitants in the 1778 Vértiz count and expanding rapidly after viceregal integration to 48k in 1813 and 68k in 1830 [@escolar2021liderazgo; @martinschlez2016medicion].

### Gobernación del Tucumán and the Potosí Trade Axis

Across the northwestern sierras and plains, the Gobernación del Tucumán (504.641 km²) remained the most populous Spanish jurisdiction east of the Andes throughout the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries [@bixio2019reflexiones; @marschoff2018movilidad]. Early indigenous populations around the Diaguita-Calchaquí valleys, Santiago del Estero and Córdoba fell from 285k in 1536 to 165k in 1600 and 118k in 1700, exacerbated by the protracted Calchaquí wars and the abandonment of exposed frontier towns such as Esteco [@marschoff2018movilidad; @bixio2019reflexiones]. Yet Tucumán possessed a resilient commercial engine: pastures in Córdoba and Santa Fe supplied young mules that were fattened in Salta and marched north each year to the Potosí silver mines, while Santiago del Estero, Catamarca and Tucumán furnished cotton cloth, leather and ox-carts [@bixio2019reflexiones; @martinschlez2016medicion]. Population rebounded to 138k in 1778, 220k in 1813 and 295k in 1830, slightly surpassing its 1536 level despite the post-1810 disruption of Upper Peruvian trade [@molina2018militarizacion].

### The Intendencia de Buenos Aires and the Río de la Plata Litoral

No territory underwent a sharper structural reversal than the Intendencia de Buenos Aires (244.799 km²). Inhabited by roughly 75k Guaraní, Chaná-Timbú and Querandí riverine foragers and horticulturalists in 1536, the littoral contracted to 42k in 1600 and 38k in 1650 as the tiny Spanish towns of Buenos Aires, Santa Fe and Corrientes struggled against indigenous resistance and isolation [@pelozattoreilly2016mano; @contente2017numeros]. Gradual *estancia* expansion, hide exports and illicit trade lifted numbers to 45k in 1700 and 58k in 1778 [@pelozattoreilly2016mano; @socolow1978merchants]. Following the 1776 creation of the viceroyalty and *Comercio Libre*, migration from the interior provinces, Spain and Africa propelled an extraordinary demographic takeoff: population more than doubled to 145k by 1813 and reached 240k in 1830 (0,98 inhabitants per km², or 0,97 on the vector mask), overtaking every Platine province except Tucumán [@johnson2011workshop; @goldberg1976poblacion; @sidy2024ninas].

### The Banda Oriental del Uruguay and the Jesuit-Guaraní Missions

The Banda Oriental and Misiones (263.007 km²) exhibited a striking mid-colonial inversion shaped by the rise and collapse of the Jesuit reductions [@kuhne2025churches; @jackson2015managing]. From 85k indigenous inhabitants in 1536, population dropped to 58k in 1600 and 52k in 1650 before recovering to 58k in 1700 as Jesuit mission towns along the Paraná and Uruguay rivers concentrated over 100k Guaraní in planned urban grids during the 1730s [@kuhne2025churches; @russel2025jesuit; @jackson2015managing]. Severe smallpox epidemics in the late 1730s, the Guaraní War (1754 to 1756) following the Treaty of Madrid and the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1767 precipitated rapid mission depopulation: major towns such as Loreto, Yapeyú, Concepción and Santa Ana lost half to three-quarters of their residents between 1731 and 1802, pulling the regional total down to 42k in 1778 [@jackson2015managing; @perezgerardo2022practicas]. Meanwhile, Montevideo (founded 1724 to 1726), Maldonado and Canelones anchored a growing Spanish-creole pastoral frontier whose cattle-hide and salted-beef economy raised the territory back to 68k in 1813 and 82k in 1830 [@fuce2017real; @gelman1905campesinos; @pollero2015que].

### Autonomous Indigenous Frontiers: Gran Chaco and Patagonia

Together, the Gran Chaco (425.650 km²) and Patagonia with the southern Pampas (1.282.338 km²) accounted for 48,6% of the study area yet remained outside effective Hispanic administration until long after 1830 [@dillehay2016reflections; @gandara2016representaciones]. Adopting the horse early in the seventeenth century transformed Guaycurú (Abipón, Mocoví and Toba) and Pampas-Tehuelche-Mapuche (*Araucanised*) bands into formidable equestrian polities that raided Santa Fe, Córdoba and the Buenos Aires frontier [@boccara1999poder; @dillehay2016reflections]. Despite equestrian mobility and cattle trading across the Andes, recurrent smallpox waves and frontier skirmishes eroded indigenous numbers steadily: the Gran Chaco declined from 185k in 1536 to 115k in 1700, 98k in 1778 and 76k in 1830, while Patagonia and the southern Pampas contracted from 110k in 1536 to 73k in 1700, 60k in 1778 and 46k in 1830 (0,04 inhabitants per km²), with Carmen de Patagones (founded 1779) standing as the sole permanent colonial outpost on the Río Negro [@gandara2016representaciones; @boccara1999politicas].

```{r tab-density, results='asis'}
dens_rows <- lapply(names(mod_data$regions), function(rk) {
  rv <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  ar <- as.numeric(rv$area_km2)
  nm <- unname(reg_short_map[rk])
  n_sites <- length(Filter(function(s) identical(s[["region_id"]], rk), sett_data))
  p1536 <- as.numeric(rv$population[["1536"]])
  p1778 <- as.numeric(rv$population[["1778"]])
  p1830 <- as.numeric(rv$population[["1830"]])
  b_low <- as.numeric(rv$population_bounds[["1830"]][[1]])
  b_high <- as.numeric(rv$population_bounds[["1830"]][[2]])
  data.frame(
    Territory = nm,
    Sites = viscount_fmt_number(n_sites, 0L),
    P1536 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1536),
    P1778 = if (rk %in% c("crp_obispado_santiago", "crp_corregimiento_cuyo")) viscount_fmt_number(p1778, 0L) else viscount_fmt_pop(p1778),
    P1830 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1830),
    Dens1830 = viscount_fmt_number(p1830 / ar, 2L),
    Bounds1830 = paste0(viscount_fmt_pop(b_low), "-", viscount_fmt_pop(b_high)),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
dens_df <- do.call(rbind, dens_rows)
rownames(dens_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  dens_df,
  "Catalogued settlements, benchmark totals, 1830 density and uncertainty ranges across the eight Southern Cone territories.",
  c("Territory", "Sites", "1536", "1778", "1830", "1830 (km²)", "1830 Bounds"),
  list(label = "tab:density-crp", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Urban Hierarchy and Atlantic Reorientation

Urbanisation across the colonial Southern Cone remained sharply constrained compared with Peru or Mexico, yet the rank-size distribution of the 177 catalogued settlements exhibits a clear power-law gradient ($\alpha = 0{,}65$, $R^2 = 0{,}95$, Figure \ref{fig:urban-crp}) [@socolow1978merchants; @johnson2011workshop]. Throughout the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, Santiago (4.865 in 1574, 11.290 in 1650 and 14.800 in 1700) was the sole settlement exceeding 10k inhabitants, functioning as the bureaucratic and agrarian capital of the Captaincy General [@valenzuelamarquez2014indios; @kamen1974mecanismes]. Córdoba (3.420 in 1614, 4.860 in 1650 and 7.283 in 1778) and Concepción (3.425 in 1574 and 6.840 in 1778) anchored the secondary tier alongside Salta (4.305 in 1778) and Mendoza (7.478 in 1778) [@bixio2019reflexiones; @escolar2021liderazgo].

```{r fig-urban, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/chile_rio_plata_banda_oriental_urban_hierarchy.png",
  "Leading recorded settlements by peak population and Zipf rank-size distribution across 177 catalogued centres.",
  "fig:urban-crp"
)
```

The late-colonial commercial realignment transformed this interior-weighted network into a bipolar Pacific-Atlantic system [@socolow1978merchants; @martinschlez2016medicion]. Buenos Aires leapt from 4.000 inhabitants in 1664 to 11.118 in 1744, 24.205 in the 1778 Vértiz census, 44.780 in 1810 and 55.416 by 1822, marginally overtaking Santiago (24.318 in 1778, 36.000 in 1813 and 54.000 in 1830) as the largest city in the region [@johnson2011workshop; @goldberg1976poblacion; @maggioramirez2019comercio]. Behind the twin capitals, maritime ports surged: Valparaíso grew from 3.420 in 1778 to 18.000 by 1830, while Montevideo rose from 340 settlers in 1726 to 4.270 in 1778 and 15.245 in 1798 before siege warfare temporarily reduced it to 9.359 in 1805 and 14.000 in 1829 [@fuce2017real; @pollero2015que; @kamen1974mecanismes]. Below these four ports and capitals, secondary towns clustered narrowly between 5k and 15k: La Isla (15k in 1779) and San Agustín de Talca (8.119) in Chile's Central Valley, Córdoba (11,5k in 1822), Mendoza (9.640 in 1812), Concepción (8.420 in 1813), Pilar Fuerte de los Ranchos (8k in 1798), the Guaraní mission capital Yapeyú (7.974 in 1768) and San Juan (7.840 in 1812) [@jackson2015managing; @contente2017numeros; @sidy2024ninas].

# Limitations

Three evidentiary constraints shape the precision of these estimates. First, pre-1776 population trajectories rely on fiscal tribute counts, ecclesiastical reports and *visita* fragments rather than comprehensive civil censuses [@valenzuelamarquez2014indios; @bixio2019reflexiones]. Tributary multipliers vary across time and social strata because *mestizaje*, *forastero* migration and *inquilinaje* continually blurred legal fiscal categories [@valenzuelamarquez2014indios; @kamen1974mecanismes]. Second, even the Bourbon censuses of 1777 to 1778 suffered asymmetric geographic omissions: the surviving Jáuregui parish breakdown omits 65.712 inhabitants included in the official Santiago diocesan total, while the Vértiz enumeration left Santiago del Estero, Corrientes, Santa Fe and the Banda Oriental to partial cabildo tallies or military padrones [@pollero2015que; @contente2017numeros]. In 1813, wartime operations prevented direct census enumeration in Santiago and Concepción provinces, forcing Egaña and later historians to interpolate across southern Chilean *partidos* [@kamen1974mecanismes].

Third, the autonomous indigenous societies of Araucanía, the Gran Chaco and Patagonia left no internal written demographic registers [@boccara1999poder; @dillehay2016reflections]. Population figures for these vast frontiers derive from Spanish missionary observations, military treaty rolls at *parlamentos*, captive testimonies and ecological carrying-capacity bounds, carrying wider true uncertainty than the colonial towns [@gandara2016representaciones; @boccara1999politicas]. Similarly, enslaved Africans and domestic *criados* in Buenos Aires, Montevideo and Santiago were frequently under-reported in household lists despite forming up to one-quarter or one-third of late-colonial urban residents [@goldberg1976poblacion; @sidy2024ninas; @johnson2011workshop].

# Conclusion

Across three centuries between 1536 and 1830, Chile, the Río de la Plata and the Banda Oriental passed through a profound demographic and spatial transformation. An indigenous population near 1,66M at first European contact contracted by more than half to 791k around 1700 under epidemic mortality, frontier warfare and forced labour transfers [@valenzuelamarquez2014indios; @boccara1999poder; @marschoff2018movilidad]. Yet unlike highland Peru, where late-colonial recovery remained constrained by altitude and agrarian saturation, the temperate valleys of Central Chile and the fertile pastoral plains of the Río de la Plata entered a sustained expansion after 1750, doubling regional numbers to 1,77M by 1830 [@kamen1974mecanismes; @gelman1905campesinos]. At the close of the colonial era, the demographic axis of the Southern Cone had tilted decisively away from the Potosí-linked interior toward the twin capitals of Santiago and Buenos Aires and their maritime outlets at Valparaíso and Montevideo, establishing the settlement framework of the modern republics [@socolow1978merchants; @fuce2017real; @martinschlez2016medicion].

# Appendix

## Chronological Anchors and Jurisdictional Realignments

Several administrative boundary shifts require explicit treatment when comparing colonial counts across time. The Corregimiento de Cuyo (Mendoza, San Juan and San Luis) formed part of the Captaincy General and Bishopric of Chile from 1561 until the creation of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata in 1776, explaining why Cuyo appears inside the 1777 to 1778 Jáuregui summary for Santiago (18.898 in Mendoza) as well as inside the 1778 Vértiz viceregal census (23.411 across all three Cuyo towns) [@escolar2021liderazgo]. Separating Cuyo into its own masked territory eliminates double-counting between Chile and the Río de la Plata in 1778 while preserving continuous sub-regional time series from 1536 to 1830.

Similarly, the thirty Jesuit-Guaraní reductions (*Misiones*) straddled the Paraná and Uruguay rivers, intersecting both Paraguayan and Platine jurisdictions before and after the 1767 expulsion [@kuhne2025churches; @russel2025jesuit]. Grouping the southern mission towns alongside the Banda Oriental reflects their shared demographic trajectory following the 1750 Treaty of Madrid, the Guaraní War and the late-eighteenth-century Portuguese-Spanish border conflicts [@jackson2015managing; @perezgerardo2022practicas; @silva1997bases]. Further west, the 1782 Ordinance of Intendants reorganised Tucumán into the twin Intendancies of Salta del Tucumán and Córdoba del Tucumán (the latter absorbing Cuyo); maintaining the historical Tucumán mask preserves longitudinal comparability with sixteenth- and seventeenth-century *visitas* [@bixio2019reflexiones; @molina2018militarizacion].

## Archival Provenance Breakdown

Across the 177 settlements compiled for this study, 116 derive primarily from the *HGIS de las Indias* (1701 to 1808) geohistorical compilation, 41 from Emilio Ravignani's edition of the 1778 *Censo de Vértiz* and supplementary Platine *padrones*, and 20 from Rolando Mellafe and Marcello Carmagnani's colonial Chilean series, with zero crowdsourced fallback entries [@kamen1974mecanismes; @contente2017numeros; @maggioramirez2019comercio]. Together with 19 archival monographs and regional demographic studies deposited in the chapter bibliography, these primary series anchor both the sub-regional totals and the 680 settlement-year population observations documented in the companion gazetteer.
